How this guide is builtBuilt from Dr. Kemp's two one-hour lectures on tubular and interstitial disease (slides and narration; references: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed.). His objectives: general clinical features of tubulointerstitial nephritis; casts and their disease associations; acute pyelonephritis (etiology, risk factors, pathology, presentation); papillary necrosis; chronic pyelonephritis; acute interstitial nephritis; and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis. Practice questions sit at the end of each section, and the lecture's own slide questions are included. beyond source = standard teaching I added; = transcript slip fixed against the slides.

1. Overview: Tubules and Interstitium

Think in compartments

  • The kidney has four compartments: glomeruli, tubules, interstitium, vasculature. Disease presents differently depending on which one is hit, which makes the differential easy to build.
  • The tubules and interstitium are separate but behave as one unit: when a disease involves one, it usually involves the other. So they are lumped together as tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) when the cause is inflammation.
  • Glomerular disease is the one that leaks protein (nephrotic/nephritic). Tubules handle water, sodium, potassium and acid, not protein, so tubulointerstitial disease shows up as electrolyte, concentration and acid-base problems.
  • Over time any compartment can spread to the others, so end-stage kidneys look alike (and glomerular disease can eventually involve tubules and vice versa).

Two main groups

  • Tubulointerstitial nephritis (cause: inflammation) → the focus of this lecture.
  • Ischemic or toxic tubular injury (clinically: acute kidney injury (AKI)) → acute tubular necrosis, covered in a separate lecture. Dr. Kemp notes it is now often called acute tubular injury, since you do not have to see necrosis to know cells are damaged.
Slide: acute vs chronic tubulointerstitial disease. The World Health Organization (WHO) lists about 15 distinct forms of tubulointerstitial nephritis, so the real world is messier than this chart.
BranchCauseDisease
Acute inflammatory damageBacterial (infectious)Acute pyelonephritis
Acute inflammatory damageImmunoglobulin E (IgE)- or T-cell-mediated (drug reaction)Drug-induced (acute) interstitial nephritis
Ischemic or toxic damageHypoperfusion or toxinAcute tubular necrosis (other lecture)
ChronicObstruction or reflux (not always or primarily infectious)Chronic pyelonephritis
ChronicSarcoidosis, heavy metals, hyperuricemia, hyperoxaluria, myelomaChronic tubulointerstitial disease
Acute vs chronic, Dr. Kemp's wayAcute tubular disease hits right now (infection, drug, ischemia). Chronic tubular disease is a low-level injury that goes on for a long time until the kidney finally fails. Chronic pyelonephritis can develop without any prior acute episode, and acute pyelonephritis does not necessarily go on to chronic.

Clinical features: tubulointerstitial vs glomerular disease

FeatureGlomerular diseaseTubulointerstitial disease
ProteinProteinuria, hypoalbuminemia (nephrotic)No significant proteinuria and no hypoalbuminemia (the tubule is not the filter)
SedimentRed blood cell (RBC) casts (nephritic)Sterile pyuria and white blood cell (WBC) casts
ConcentrationUsually preserved earlyConcentrating defect: polyuria and nocturia
Other tubular defects—Renal tubular acidosis (RTA), salt-losing nephropathy, osteomalacia (vitamin D deficiency)
Exception from narration"Sterile" pyuria applies to the inflammatory forms (drug-induced, chronic). Acute pyelonephritis is the exception: it is a real infection, and WBC casts there come with bacteria in the urine.

2. Casts and Crystals

  • A cast is a mold of the renal tubule (protein matrix plus trapped material), so a cast always means the material came from the kidney. Dr. Kemp: casts are very characteristic of specific disorders, so know them.
Cast / crystalAssociated diseaseMemory hook
RBC castGlomerulonephritis (nephritic syndrome, rapidly progressive disease)Blood coming from the glomerulus
WBC castInfection of the kidney (acute pyelonephritis) and interstitial nephritisInflammation in the tubulointerstitium
Pigmented granular ("muddy brown") castAcute tubular injury (necrosis)Dead cells sloughing into the tubule
Cellular cast (renal tubular epithelial cells)Acute tubular injury (necrosis)Same story
Waxy castChronic renal failureOld, stagnant cast
Fatty castNephrotic syndromeLiver overmakes lipoprotein to offset albumin loss, so lipid spills into urine
Hyaline castMay be normalTamm-Horsfall protein only
Oxalate crystalsCalcium oxalate is the most common stone; also seen with ethylene glycol ingestionEnvelope-shaped
Slide: waxy casts, RBC casts, cellular cast, and oxalate crystals.
Exam tipDr. Kemp expects stems to give you enough information (history, labs) rather than just a picture, but the cast-to-disease pairs above are the testable content.

3. Acute Pyelonephritis

Pyelo- = pelvis: the inflammation is in the renal pelvis and the kidney around it. Basic description: an acute infection, usually bacterial, of the kidney.

Etiology

  • Escherichia coli in 73–82% of cases. The anus and urethra are close together, so it is easy for E. coli to cross over.

Risk factors

SourceRisk factors
Robbins (slide)Female > male; urinary obstruction; instrumentation; vesicoureteral reflux (VUR), congenital or acquired (spinal cord or peripheral nerve injury); pregnancy; diabetes mellitus; immunosuppression or immunodeficiency
Colgan and Williams (2011) (slide)Sexual intercourse three or more times per week, urinary tract infection (UTI) in the past 12 months, diabetes mellitus, stress incontinence. Pregnancy not listed.
  • Reflux is the key link: cystitis does not simply ascend to the kidney. You need a problem at the vesicoureteral junction (VUR) for infection to travel up the ureter. Obstruction lets urine sit, and anything sitting can get infected.
  • Diabetes behaves like low-level immunosuppression, and high urine sugar feeds bacterial growth.
  • Most cases ascend from the bladder, but hematogenous spread is possible (e.g., endocarditis, pneumonia).
Points to ponder: the two sources disagreeRobbins: "4–6% of pregnant women develop bacteriuria sometime during pregnancy, and 20–40% of these eventually develop symptomatic urinary tract infection if not treated," and lists pregnancy as a predisposing condition. Colgan and Williams: "Although acute pyelonephritis also occurs in men, children, and pregnant women, these groups account for only a small percentage of cases." Dr. Kemp's point: summaries of the same data can reach different conclusions, and "rare" to one author is "common" to another. For exams, use the Robbins list.

Pathology

  • Abscess formation, usually unilateral (yellow pus collections in the cortex on gross).
  • Microscopic: tubules filled with neutrophils. The glomeruli are surprisingly resistant (inflammation all around, but not in them), though they can become involved in severe cases, giving some proteinuria.
Slide: acute pyelonephritis. Febrile patient with costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness and a previous UTI; arrows mark the lesions.
Slide: abscesses (arrows) in acute pyelonephritis.
vesicoureteral reflux on one side only.">
Slide: same individual, "Why difference?" Left kidney has no pyelonephritis; right kidney has severe pyelonephritis. The best explanation is vesicoureteral reflux on one side only.
Slide: microscopy, tubule filled with neutrophils.

Clinical presentation

  • Any age. From infancy to about 40 years, incidence is higher in females (shorter distance from the body surface to the bladder). Males in this window usually have a congenital anomaly, so they present earlier. After about 40, male incidence rises because of urinary obstruction (e.g., benign prostatic hyperplasia).
  • Costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness (the inflamed kidney hurts when you tap the flank).
  • Systemic infection: fever, chills, nausea, malaise, plus dysuria, frequency, urgency.
  • Urinalysis: pyuria, bacteria, WBC casts. beyond source
Cystitis vs pyelonephritisCystitis (bladder): frequency, urgency, dysuria, maybe blood, but no systemic features. Once the infection reaches the kidney, fever, chills and CVA tenderness appear.

4. Papillary Necrosis

  • Basic description: necrosis of the renal papillae.
  • Predisposing conditions (memorize): diabetes mellitus, urinary tract obstruction, analgesic abuse, sickle cell anemia.
  • Pathology: ischemic injury with suppurative necrosis of the papillae. The dead tissue may slough and obstruct the ureter.
  • It occurs on its own and as a component of acute pyelonephritis (the way Dr. Kemp has most often seen it).
  • Sickle cell: sickled cells block the small vessels that supply the papillae → ischemia → necrosis.
Slide: papillary necrosis. Gross specimen with yellow necrotic papillae rimmed by red hyperemia; inset shows microscopy.

5. Chronic Pyelonephritis

  • Basic description: chronic kidney disease caused by recurrent inflammation from obstruction or reflux. It is a cause of chronic renal failure and hypertension (the kidney helps maintain blood pressure).
  • It does not require previous acute pyelonephritis.
  • Usually a lower-grade, recurrent infection, more like bronchiectasis than a dramatic acute attack.
Chronic obstructive pyelonephritisChronic reflux-associated pyelonephritis
SettingRecurrent infection on a background of obstructionRecurrent UTIs on a background of reflux (most often congenital VUR)
ResultMultiple episodes of inflammation → scarringMultiple episodes of inflammation → scarring
LateralityBilateral or unilateralBilateral or unilateral
Points from the slidesA PubMed search did not find the exact term "chronic reflux-associated pyelonephritis"; the obstructive form has a New England Journal of Medicine image case. In a 1977 series (Salvatierra and Tanagho), 32 patients with reflux (10 sterile reflux, 22 reflux with recurrent UTIs) all developed end-stage renal failure. Take-away: reflux can damage the kidney even without infection, and reflux can be unilateral, so one kidney can be scarred and the other normal.

Pathology

  • Gross: unilateral or bilateral, unequal scarring of the cortex, often at the poles, with blunting of the underlying calyx.
  • Microscopic: patchy fibrosis and chronic inflammatory infiltrates (lymphocytes, plasma cells), tubular atrophy, globally sclerotic glomeruli, and thyroidization of the tubules.
  • Thyroidization = tubules distended with pink colloid-like material so they look like thyroid follicles. It is characteristic but not absolutely specific for chronic pyelonephritis.
Slide: scar at renal pole (arrow).
Slide: same person. Normal-appearing kidney on the left, small atrophic scarred kidney on the right (unilateral disease).
Slide: both kidneys scarred (black arrows indicate scarred areas).
Slide: thyroidization of the tubules, lymphocytes, and globally sclerotic glomeruli.
Slide: thyroidization of the tubules, low power (left) and higher power (right).
Dr. Kemp's caveat from narrationOn gross exam it can be hard to tell chronic pyelonephritis from an old infarct scar: both show loss of the cortical surface, some blunting of the calyx, and both can involve the poles. Interpret the gross with history and microscopy. Tubular atrophy = tubules no longer back to back; lymphocytes, atrophy and fibrosis are nonspecific changes of chronic kidney disease.

Clinical presentation

  • Gradual onset of renal failure.
  • Inability to concentrate the urine (hyposthenuria) → polyuria and nocturia, because loss of tubules causes tubular dysfunction and loss of concentrating ability. Sodium and water regulation is also impaired.
  • Secondary glomerular disease can develop later → proteinuria (usually mild, e.g., 1+).

Acute vs chronic renal failure

HistoryKidneysHemoglobinBone x-ray
Acute kidney injuryPreviously normal blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinineNormal sizeNormalNormal
Chronic renal diseaseElevated BUN and creatinine in the pastSmallerDecreased (less erythropoietin)Renal osteodystrophy (vitamin D and mineral disturbance)

Chronic disease = small kidneys, anemia, bone disease; acute = normal-sized kidneys, normal hemoglobin and bone.

6. Acute (Drug-Induced) Interstitial Nephritis

  • Basic description: inflammation of the renal interstitium associated with drug use. Patients often have fever, eosinophilia, rash and renal abnormalities about 2 weeks (about 15 days) after starting the drug.
  • It is not an infection (so there is no bacteria in the urine and no "pyelo").

Etiology

  • Synthetic penicillins (methicillin, ampicillin), diuretics, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and many others.

Pathogenesis

  • Type I (IgE) and/or type IV (T-cell) hypersensitivity.
  • The drug acts as a hapten: it is secreted by the tubules, binds a cytoplasmic or extracellular component, and triggers an IgE and/or cell-mediated immune reaction against the tubulointerstitium.

Clinical presentation

  • Fever, eosinophilia, rash, renal dysfunction about 15 days after exposure; hematuria, leukocyturia (WBC casts) and a little proteinuria may be seen. Urine output may fall.
  • Reality check (Kodner and Kudrimoti, 2003): the clinical picture is just acute renal failure from any cause. Except for a history of new medication or illness, nothing in the history, exam or labs reliably distinguishes it. The classic fever, rash and arthralgias may be absent in up to two thirds of patients. Urine eosinophils and renal gallium-67 scanning are suggestive but cannot confirm or exclude it. Renal biopsy is the gold standard.
  • Practical point: when a patient has a rising BUN and creatinine, always ask about new medications.

Epidemiology

  • Up to 1% of renal biopsies done for hematuria or proteinuria show acute interstitial nephritis.
  • 5–15% of people hospitalized for acute kidney injury have it.

Pathology (microscopic)

  • Interstitial edema (space between tubules).
  • Infiltrate of lymphocytes and macrophages; can include eosinophils (the most characteristic cell) and neutrophils; occasional granulomas.
  • Pathologist's caveat: a lymphocytic infiltrate alone does not prove "acute," because chronic cells appear in acute drug reactions. You need the history; scarring or small kidneys point to a chronic process.
Slide: acute drug-induced interstitial nephritis (arrows indicate eosinophils).
Points to ponder (Dr. Kemp's answers)Why little or no proteinuria? The injury is in the tubulointerstitium, whose job is not to handle protein; the glomeruli (the filter) are spared, at least early. How often is a biopsy done? Not often: biopsy is the gold standard, but because of its risks (bleeding), it is usually reserved for when the cause of acute kidney injury is unclear. A typical history with other causes ruled out is often enough.

7. Chronic Tubulointerstitial Nephritis

  • General description: chronic kidney disease (CKD) from low-level, not acutely toxic, exposure to a substance over time. Patients present gradually, once enough kidney is lost.
  • Pathology: interstitial inflammatory infiltrate, fibrosis, tubular atrophy (space between tubules). The kidney is smaller than normal.
  • Clinical presentation: gradual renal dysfunction (concentrating defect, polyuria and nocturia, tubular acidosis).

Etiologies

CategoryExamples
Analgesic nephropathy (common worldwide)Aspirin combined with phenacetin, caffeine or acetaminophen
Immune-mediatedSarcoidosis
ToxinsLead, cadmium
MetabolicHyperuricemia, hyperoxaluria, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia
MalignancyMultiple myeloma
Slide: chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis. Tubular atrophy (blue arrow) and chronic inflammatory cells (yellow arrows); fibrosis.
Acute vs chronic drug nephritisAcute drug-induced interstitial nephritis shows up within days to weeks of a new drug; chronic disease builds over months to years from low-level exposure. Both can look lymphocytic on microscopy, so the history separates them.

8. Cast and Cast-like Disorders of the Tubules

Some conditions plug the tubules with material and damage the kidney slowly over time. Dr. Kemp lists four: hemolysis (hemoglobin), rhabdomyolysis (myoglobin), multiple myeloma (light chains) and nephrocalcinosis (calcium deposits). Like chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis, they typically present with gradual loss of renal function and chronic kidney disease.

Slide: cast in multiple myeloma (casts often appear cracked).
Slide: nephrocalcinosis (calcium deposits in the renal parenchyma), low power.
Slide: nephrocalcinosis (arrow marks a calcium deposit), higher power.
CauseWhat plugs or depositsHook
HemolysisFree hemoglobinHeme pigment, dark urine
RhabdomyolysisMyoglobinDipstick positive for blood without RBCs; high creatine kinase
Multiple myelomaMonoclonal light chainsCracked-looking casts; dipstick can be negative for protein
NephrocalcinosisCalcium (calcium phosphate or oxalate) in tubules and parenchymaSeen with hypercalcemia, hyperoxaluria and type 1 renal tubular acidosis

The last-row hook and the pigment/enzyme details are standard teaching points I added. beyond source

9. Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA)

Dr. Kemp's noteStudents asked him to include RTA because it shows up on other exams; he said it will not be on his questions, but it is useful for understanding tubule function. The diagrams below are his own drawings: red = primary mechanism, yellow = secondary effect. There is no type 3 on his list.

In RTA a tubular transport defect causes a metabolic acidosis while the glomerular filtration rate is relatively preserved. The type depends on where the defect is.

Type 1: distalType 2: proximalType 4: hyperkalemic
Primary defectAlpha-intercalated cell cannot secrete H⁺, so new HCO₃⁻ is not madeProximal tubule cannot reabsorb HCO₃⁻ (carbonic anhydrase defect on the slide); can be isolated or part of Fanconi syndrome (other proximal functions lost too)Aldosterone deficiency or resistance: Na⁺ reabsorption (and so K⁺ secretion) fails
PotassiumLow (hypokalemia)Low (hypokalemia)High (hyperkalemia); high K⁺ blocks NH₃ production, so less NH₄⁺ is excreted
UrineAlkaline (cannot acidify)Can still acidify (distal H⁺ secretion is intact)Can acidify (urine pH usually below 5.5) beyond source
OtherCalcium and citrate lost in urine → nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosisPhosphate, glucose, amino acids lost if FanconiMild acidosis
Causes beyond sourceSjögren syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, amphotericin BFanconi syndrome, multiple myeloma, heavy metals, acetazolamide, topiramateDiabetic nephropathy (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism), Addison disease, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Slide: type 1 (distal) RTA, drawn in the alpha-intercalated cell. H⁺ secretion is blocked, giving decreased HCO₃⁻ (metabolic acidosis), alkaline urine, hypokalemia, and loss of calcium and citrate (nephrolithiasis).
Slide: type 2 (proximal) RTA. The carbonic anhydrase/HCO₃⁻ step in the proximal tubule is blocked; secondary hypokalemia; distal acidification is still intact. Isolated type 2 RTA vs Fanconi syndrome (other proximal reabsorption lost too).
Slide: type 4 RTA, aldosterone deficiency or resistance. Blocked Na⁺ reabsorption means blocked K⁺ secretion (hyperkalemia), and the hyperkalemia blocks NH₃ production (possibly via effects of K⁺ on the ammonia transporter).

Tubulointerstitial vs glomerularRemember
ProteinGlomerular = proteinuria; tubulointerstitial = little or none
CastsRBC = glomerulonephritis; WBC = pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis; muddy = acute tubular injury; waxy = chronic renal failure; fatty = nephrotic
Function lostTubular: concentration, sodium, acid, vitamin D (polyuria, nocturia, RTA, salt wasting, osteomalacia)
Acute vs chronic kidney diseaseAcute: normal-size kidneys, normal hemoglobin, normal bone. Chronic: small kidneys, anemia, renal osteodystrophy
